perPress.answerFull:
**Positional encoding** in this paper uses fixed sine and cosine functions of different frequencies, added to the input embeddings. For position `pos` and dimension `i`:

$$PE_{(pos, 2i)} = \sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{model}}}\right)$$
$$PE_{(pos, 2i+1)} = \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{model}}}\right)$$

The wavelengths form a geometric progression from $2\pi$ up to $10000 \cdot 2\pi$.

The reason behind choosing sine and cosine is that it lets the model easily learn to attend by **relative positions**. Because of the trig identity $\sin(a+b) = \sin(a)\cos(b) + \cos(a)\sin(b)$, for any fixed offset $k$, $PE_{pos+k}$ can be written as a linear function of $PE_{pos}$. So the model doesn't have to memorize absolute positions, it can pick up on "how far apart" two tokens are using simple linear combinations. They also tried learned positional embeddings and got nearly identical results, so sine/cosine was kept as the default since it works without extra parameters and generalizes to longer sequences than those seen in training.

perPress.label: long-range-multihead-cost-rationale
perPress.answerPreview: **Multi-head attention** keeps the total cost roughly the same as single-head attention because each head works on a smaller slice of the embedding rather than the full thing. So instead of one attention layer doing a $d_{model}$-dimensional projection, you do $h$ heads in parallel, each projecting
perPress.answerFull:
**Multi-head attention** keeps the total cost roughly the same as single-head attention because each head works on a smaller slice of the embedding rather than the full thing. So instead of one attention layer doing a $d_{model}$-dimensional projection, you do $h$ heads in parallel, each projecting into $d_{model}/h$ dimensions.

Concretely, a single dot-product attention takes $Q K^\top$ where the per-token vectors are $d_k$ wide, so the work scales like $d_k^2$ per head. With 8 heads at $d_k = 64$, each head does $64^2 = 4096$ units of work, and $8 \times 4096 = 32768$. Compare that to one head at full $d_{model} = 512$, which is $512^2 = 262144$. So multi-head is actually way cheaper per head, and the 8 heads together still come out cheaper than one full-width head.

The trick is the parameter matrices $W_i^Q, W_i^K, W_i^V$ still map from the full $d_{model}$, so each head sees the whole input, just in a lower-dimensional projection space. Then you concatenate the $h$ outputs and let $W^O$ mix them back into $d_{model}$. Net effect: similar parameter count, similar FLOPs, but the model gets to attend to information from $h$ different representation subspaces at once, which is what makes it more expressive than a single head of the same total width.

There's the self-attention layer, which is similar to the encoder's in that queries, keys, and values all come from the same previous decoder layer. But on top of that, there's an extra attention sub-layer the e
perPress.answerFull:
So the decoder actually has two flavors of attention happening, not just self-attention. There's the self-attention layer, which is similar to the encoder's in that queries, keys, and values all come from the same previous decoder layer. But on top of that, there's an extra attention sub-layer the encoder doesn't have, called encoder-decoder attention. In that one, the queries come from the decoder, but the keys and values come from the encoder's output. That's what lets each decoder position look back at the entire input sequence.

The other big difference is masking. The decoder's self-attention is modified so that positions can't attend to future positions. Combined with shifting the output embeddings by one, this keeps the prediction autoregressive, meaning position $i$ can only depend on known outputs at positions before $i$.

So on the question of whether it generalizes well beyond translation: the authors only really stress-test it on constituency parsing, which is encouraging but a narrow sample. The architecture has no recurrence or convolution, so in principle it should be domain-agnostic since attention doesn't care about the structure of the input. In practice, though, position information has to be added back in (sinusoidal embeddings here), and tasks with very different input/output layouts, like image generation or reinforcement learning, would need those position schemes reworked. The paper shows the idea is portable, not that it solves everything.
